findings.description: The Lambda function embeds a long-lived AWS access key ID and secret access key as plaintext environment variables in the Terraform configuration. These credentials are committed to source control, stored in cleartext in Terraform state, and readable by any principal with lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration or console access to the function.

No kms_key_arn is set, so the environment variables holding these secrets are protected only by the default AWS-managed key and are transparently decrypted for anyone able to read the function configuration. A customer-managed CMK with a restricted key policy would add a second access-control boundary around the secrets.
The function targets the nodejs12.x runtime, which has reached end of life and no longer receives security patches from AWS, leaving known vulnerabilities in the execution environment unremediated.

No vpc_config block is defined, so the function runs outside any customer VPC with unrestricted outbound internet egress and no security group or subnet boundary. Combined with the embedded static AWS credentials, this makes exfiltration of those secrets to an attacker-controlled endpoint trivial if the function code or a dependency is compromised.

The assume-role policy grants sts:AssumeRole to the lambda.amazonaws.com service principal with no aws:SourceAccount or aws:SourceArn condition, so the trust relationship is not scoped to a specific account or function ARN. This is a defence-in-depth gap against confused-deputy style abuse of the service principal.
